He Bought a Chevy Corvette for $137,000, Drove 562 Miles, Sold for $99,500
25 photos
Photo: Cars and Bids
Depreciation is a killer, and it affects luxury and sports cars most, unless they are rare, exclusive models. The owner of this 2025 Chevrolet Corvette E-Ray convertible learned it the hard way. He paid $136,890 to drive it off the showroom floor. One year and 572 miles later, he sold it for $37,000 under the sticker.
The original owner bought this Chevrolet Corvette E-Ray 3LZ convertible back in August 2025 and was planning to have fun with it. However life happened and here it is, hardly broken in and already sold. He chose Arctic White for the exterior and Jet Black with contrasting Adrenaline Red stitching and Torch Red seatbelts for the interior. The cabin is sheltered by a power retractable hardtop.
The one-year-old Chevy Corvette rides on five-spoke wheels finished in black, measuring 20 inches up front and 21 inches out back, hiding red-painted brake calipers. The car features the very much appreciated front-axle lift system with memory function for peace of mind when coming across speed bumps and sits on the Magnetic Selective Ride Control.
Photo: Cars and Bids The E-Ray was the first hybrid Corvette with all-wheel drive ever to see the light of day. In the meantime, General Motors pulled the plug on it to make room for the Corvette Grand Sport X, which comes with the brand-new 6.7-liter V8. But the E-Ray is powered by the 6.2-liter LT2 V8 and an electric motor.
Together, they push 655 horsepower (664 metric horsepower) and 595 pound-feet (807 Newton meters) of torque. That is enough to make the hybrid Corvette flash from 0 to 60 mph (0 to 97 kph) in 2.5 seconds, run the quarter mile in 10.5 seconds with a trap speed of 130 mph (209 kph) and max out at 183 mph (295 kph).
An eight-speed automatic transmission puts the power down through all four corners. A tiny 1.9-kWh battery stores enough energy for a very short drive of 3 to 4 miles (5 to 6.5 kilometers) on electric power only.
However, the original owner didn't even get to enjoy much of that performance. After one year and three months, he listed the Corvette for sale with just 562 miles (905 kilometers) on the clock. However, it does make sense. He has a family of four and two "fun cars." With two kids having "too much going on," he is not left with much time to drive the two-seater.
Photo: Cars and Bids So he already got rid of it. For $99,500, which is roughly $37,000 under the sticker, the buyer is getting a very low-mileage car, two key fobs, the manuals, the window sticker, the trickle charger, and a serialized crystal glass model. The Carfax report shows a clean history and no mileage discrepancies. No surprise there! The 'Vette hasn't even required service yet. Steal or deal? What do you think?
